newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan shares volume buttressed by Arab Bank.
newsitem.headline: Jordan shares volume buttressed by Arab Bank.

text.p: Institutional demand on Arab Bank helped pushed Amman's bourse turnover higher on Sunday but continued lack of buying impetus dragged it down 0.58 percent, brokers said.
"There were offers to sell Arab Bank with unusually strong demand for large quantities by big investors, most probably the social security corporation (state pension fund)," said one broker.
The official Amman Financial Market (AFM) index shed 89 points to 152.86 points, its lowest level since January, in high 1,039,111 dinar ($1,467,000) turnover.
Arab Bank, which dropped 1.50 dinars to 254.75 dinars in trade worth 687,525 dinars, alone accounted for more than two thirds of Sunday's trading volume.

Brokers said mostly institutional buyers found attractively priced large chunks of Arab Bank in block sales by sellers whose enthusiasm waned after rumours the bank may not announce in 1997 a widely expected bonus share after delays in approval of a new companies law despite having been passed by parliament.
Leading Arab Bank's share has been buttressed since the government said it will eliminate a 15 percent tax on capitalisation through reserves in a new companies law. The
bank's management had tied a pledge of a bonus share to the passing of the law but gave no date when it planned to make the move.

Renewed uncertainty over the fate of Middle East peace added to investor worries about the fate of $120 million worth of orders won by Jordanian firms under the U.N. "oil-for food" deal, which have yet to be approved by the sanctions committee.
Many industrial firms, especially drug manufacturers, hope Iraq exports will boost performance and use idle capacity.
Some recent buying has been motivated by expectations Iraq orders will produce improved 1997 results.
Growing doubts about the government's seriousness in implementing its privatisation pledge continues to hold back investors, dealers say.
Only a handful of bluechips continued to bolster the market in across the board price slides in most of the less popular shares.
The second and third busiest shares, Unified Transport Company and Bank of Jordan fell 0.03 dinars to 1.65 dinars and 0.02 dinars to 2.86 dinars respectively.
Drug bluechip Dar al-Dawa which recently saw some limited foreign investor interest, was unchanged at 4.78 dinars in trade worth only 21,743 dinars.
Only six stocks rose against 25 declines on Sunday, while nine traded but closed unchanged.
The private Pearl Index of the 45 most-traded shares on the exchange shed 0.63 percent to 80.25 points, 3.77 percent down from the start of the year.
